title: AI apps haven't broken out — it's not a product problem, it's a model problem
dek: More than a year after GPT-4, Perplexity is the only AI app from mainstream Silicon Valley VCs to reach 20 million-plus monthly actives; 90% of the reason is that GPT-4-level capability isn't enough — it can only do information synthesis, not long-horizon reasoning.
why: Someone long based in the US reviews half a year of the AI app ecosystem, with details on Perplexity's fundraising, retention and moat, and the physical reason GPT-5 is slow. High information density, specific judgments.
who: VCs watching AI app investment and startups, AI product leads hunting for PMF, and technical and strategy people who want to understand why GPT-5 is slow and whether the large-model business model holds up.
skip: After 1:03:32, the China-US innovation ecosystem comparison is fairly general and can be skipped.

points.h: A year after GPT-4, AI apps are still boring
points.body: The guest's biggest takeaway from the first half of the year: more than a year after GPT-4 came out, AI apps still haven't had a big breakout, and judged by results it's fairly boring. Setting aside the large-model companies' own apps, among AI apps backed by mainstream Silicon Valley VCs and reaching a meaningful valuation, he can only think of Perplexity — 20 million-plus monthly actives, 20 million-plus USD ARR, and by year-end possibly 100 million monthly actives and 100 million USD ARR. Many other companies are still pre-PMF. This judgment is the starting point for the whole episode's discussion: it's not that app teams aren't working hard, it's that the available model capability can't yet support anything bigger.

points.h: Information retrieval is the use case that best matches model capability today
points.body: The guest divides knowledge workers' creative tasks into three types: combinatorial creativity, exploratory creativity, and transformative creativity. Information retrieval belongs to combinatorial creativity, the capability today's models match best; writing a Tesla investment research report belongs to exploratory creativity, which also requires planning and reasoning; discovering the law of universal gravitation belongs to transformative creativity, and today's large models still struggle to generalize from one case to others and handle things they haven't seen. So the complex information Q&A Perplexity does happens to fit existing model capability — a relatively fit PMF. He also mentions education as possibly the second matching scenario.

points.h: AI search only needs to take one or two points from Google to be huge
points.body: Perplexity's latest round valued it at 3 billion USD, and the guest explains why it's worth that much: search is still the fattest, biggest market on the internet. Microsoft Bing has only 3.4% of global search share, yet generates 12 billion USD in annual revenue. So if AI search takes just 1% to 2% of Google's share, the business is already very big. He also notes that Perplexity's search queries per active user per day are more than three times Google's, and its long-term retention is significantly higher than other AI products; Toutiao's app in 2013 had roughly 46% next-day retention, and Perplexity's retention is basically the same.

points.h: Perplexity has an 80% chance of being acquired
points.body: Asked about Perplexity's endgame, the guest says there's an 80% chance it gets acquired. The reason: startups today all seem to live under the giants' radiation, and this is a core battleground. He cites Meta's glasses integrating a voice version of Perplexity, Siri borrowing a search engine, and Microsoft Bing working at it for ages without earning that good a reputation, while Perplexity's reputation is actually very good. On the moat, he thinks it's the user mindshare created by first-mover effects. At the same time he admits Perplexity still has a lot of room to explore in usage frequency, monetization, and how to compete with the giants without colliding head-on.

points.h: Apps haven't broken out — 90% of it is model capability falling short
points.body: The guest splits the reasons AI-native apps haven't had a systemic breakout into two parts: 90% is that GPT-4-level capability isn't enough — it can only do innovation like information synthesis, and can't do long-horizon reasoning or creative work, so everyone still has to grind on the next generation of models, especially reasoning and multimodal capability; the remaining 10% may be a matter of time — based only on GPT-4-level capability, there's still a chance of building a big app in the future. He cites NLP taking twenty years to give birth to search, and electricity first producing the light bulb as its killer app, and thinks that after more than a year of polishing, everyone is close to something that feels like PMF — but this needs young product geniuses.

points.h: GPT-5 is slow because of GPU construction in the physical world
points.body: The guest argues GPT-5 being slower than expected is not an AI problem, not a data shortage, and not the scaling law hitting a wall, but a real GPU construction problem in the physical world. GPT-4 was a several-dozen-fold compute increase over GPT-3, while GPT-5 today is only a ten-plus-fold compute increase over GPT-4. H100s only arrived in large volumes in Q4 2023, building clusters takes a lot of time, large GPU clusters are still unstable, and large-scale training only became possible early this year; from getting GPUs to actually being able to train at scale takes another half year. He expects GPT-5 by year-end, with parameters three to five times larger than GPT-4 and data volume seven or eight to ten times larger.

points.h: Large models aren't a good business model — ad platforms are
points.body: The guest states plainly that large models are definitely not a better business model than ad platforms right now. ChatGPT has over 100 million DAU; assuming 10% pay and 200 USD a year, that's 2 billion USD — still just 1% to 2% of Google's ad platform revenue of over 200 billion USD a year. An ad platform can earn back a new user within 6 to 12 months, with clearly calculable ROI; the ROI of buying GPUs for large models can't be calculated, and it combines research attributes with a high failure rate. But he also points out that OpenAI has actually long since earned back its training costs through ChatGPT, and the losses are mainly in exploring new model technology — much like a pharma company's new drug R&D.

points.h: Startups and big companies are a dependency relationship, not a disruption relationship
points.body: The guest sums up: startups and big companies are not a disruption relationship but a dependency relationship. Reason one is that AI companies still burn too much money; reason two is that the giants are too well positioned. He cites OpenAI: GPUs are constrained by Nvidia, cluster building is constrained by Microsoft, Microsoft is also a 49% major shareholder and backer, Azure is the most important channel to enterprise customers, and on the consumer side it can't escape Apple — in the end it still has to kneel to Apple to get in, while Apple can swap out ChatGPT in a minute. So if OpenAI really wants to disrupt, it seems it can only take a shot at Google. This also explains why the giants are all potentially still beneficiaries.

quotes.text: It's been more than a year since GPT-4 came out, and AI apps still haven't had a big breakout — judged by results, it's fairly boring.
Information retrieval is still the most important use case that matches model capability.
Look at startups and big companies — it seems to be not a disruption relationship but a dependency relationship.
